To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) particulate aluminium in surface waters is removed from the surface layer at a rate of about 10 m d−1; (ii) this removal rate is consistent with first-order removal; and (iii) this first-order removal may be caused by filter-feeding salps.
the vertical distribution of aluminium in surface waters of the Gulf Stream is consistent with that predicted by a simple model of particle removal from surface layers by a first-order process.
the distribution of particulate aluminum in the Gulf Stream is consistent with that of a particle with first-order removal in the upper 150 meters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the chemical composition of aerosol particles and their interaction with the oceanic surface layer.
the processes which remove particulate aluminium from oceanic surface layers, and the implications this has for the cycling of particulate aluminium and other trace metals in oceanic surface waters.
understanding the role of the ocean in global cycles of chemical elements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the vertical distribution of Al is consistent with the hypothesis that primary input is from the atmosphere and that first-order removal occurs in the upper 200 m of the water.
the removal of small particles is an important mechanism in the ocean, but that the precise mechanism(s) involved are not known.
the removal of small particulate matter from surface waters of the oceans is a first-order process and is probably caused by the feeding activities of zooplankton.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the vertical distribution of aluminium is consistent with a model of first-order removal in the upper 50 m of the water.
the removal of particulate aluminum from surface waters is consistent with the hypothesis of removal by filter feeders.
the vertical distribution of particles in the ocean may be more closely related to biological processes than previously recognized.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have demonstrated the feasibility of using particulate aluminium as a tracer for particle fluxes in the upper ocean, and that the vertical distribution of aluminium is consistent with the hypothesis that salps play an important role in particle export.

filter-feeding zooplankton can have a significant impact on the distribution of trace metals in surface waters, and that these effects need to be taken into account when interpreting the geochemical cycling and distribution of trace metals.

we have found evidence that the removal rate of small particulate aluminium in surface layers is much higher than previously assumed, and that this is consistent with the removal of other small particles.
